stories.title: Sam Altman on Nvidia without Jensen Huang: The industry will be ‘fine’
stories.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman acknowledged the special role Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has played in the AI boom, but ultimately thinks the industry will be “fine” without him at the helm.

sources.name: TechCrunch AI
sources.title: Sam Altman on Nvidia without Jensen Huang: The industry will be ‘fine’
sources.text: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says the AI industry will be “fine” without Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at the helm, even as he acknowledged the special role Huang has played in the AI boom. Huang resigned last week from Nvidia after admitting to having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Altman made his first public comments about Huang’s departure on Monday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event, where he also discussed topics ranging from data center pushback to recursive self-improvement. Numerous executives and members of the AI industry have argued for Nvidia to reinstate Huang, including Elon Musk and Epic Games chief executive Tim Sweeney, who were among the signatories in a public letter. Many fear that Huang’s departure may cause Nvidia to rethink the enormous financial risks it has taken that have fueled the AI boom. Huang is also reportedly setting up a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for his return. When asked whether he thought Huang should return to the company, Altman said: “I don’t think I know enough to answer that question.” He expressed empathy for Huang’s situation, citing his own ousting from OpenAI in 2023 after board members accused him of withholding information. “It’s hard to imagine the AI revolution without Jensen and the company he has built,” Altman said, adding that he sees Huang as a hero, and that “heroes have flaws.” OpenAI and Nvidia have had a close relationship for the last decade, one that has evolved from a simple chip supplier-customer relationship into a potentially circular financing arrangement, in which Nvidia’s money helps fund purchases of its own chips. Most recently, Nvidia agreed to provide a guarantee of up to $105 billion backing OpenAI’s Ohio data center project. That’s just one of many such circular deals Nvidia has made to bankroll the AI boom while fueling demand for its own chips. Altman said he’s not worried that the Bank of Nvidia will dry up. “Nvidia is, like, a behemoth of a company,” he said. “I think people still trust their guarantees very much.” Altman acknowledged the “ambition” Huang brought to the industry, the scale of which “has been quite important.” But he didn’t go so far as to agree with the many who worry about ripple effects from Huang’s departure. “I think there’s so much demand, and it’s so clear that AI is real, and people want to use it, and the revenues and demand are growing so strongly that I think the industry will be fine,” Altman said. “But again, I think Jensen has played this extremely special and valuable role as someone to really drive things forward with great ambition.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . This doesn’t affect our editorial independence. Rebecca Bellan is a senior reporter at TechCrunch where she covers the business, policy, and emerging trends shaping artificial intelligence. Her work has also appeared in Forbes, Bloomberg, The Atlantic, The Daily Beast, and other publications. You can contact or verify outreach from Rebecca by emailing [email protected] or via encrypted message at rebeccabellan.491 on Signal. sources.name: Olhar Digital IA
sources.title: Sam Altman diz que indústria de IA ficará bem sem Jensen Huang na Nvidia
sources.text: O CEO da OpenAI, Sam Altman, acredita que a indústria de inteligência artificial (IA) continuará avançando mesmo sem Jensen Huang no comando da Nvidia . Apesar de reconhecer a importância do executivo para o desenvolvimento do setor, ele afirmou que a demanda por IA é forte o suficiente para manter o mercado em expansão. As declarações foram feitas nesta segunda-feira (16), durante o evento Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World . Foi a primeira vez que Altman comentou publicamente a saída de Huang da fabricante de chips, após o executivo deixar o cargo de CEO na semana passada. Questionado sobre a possibilidade de o fundador retornar à liderança da Nvidia, Altman evitou tomar partido. “Não acho que eu saiba o suficiente para responder a essa pergunta”, afirmou. A declaração de Altman também chama atenção pela relação comercial entre as duas empresas. A Nvidia é uma das principais fornecedoras de chips utilizados no desenvolvimento e na operação de sistemas de IA da OpenAI. Mais recentemente, a fabricante concordou em oferecer garantias de até US$ 105 bilhões (cerca de R$ 560 bilhões) para respaldar o projeto de data center da OpenAI em Ohio. O acordo faz parte de relação financeira mais complexa entre as companhias. A Nvidia investe no crescimento do mercado de IA e, ao mesmo tempo, ajuda a financiar empresas que compram seus próprios chips. Questionado sobre a possibilidade de a saída de Huang afetar esse tipo de financiamento, Altman disse não estar preocupado. Segundo ele, a Nvidia é uma empresa gigantesca e suas garantias continuam inspirando confiança no mercado. Altman reconheceu que a ambição de Huang e sua capacidade de impulsionar grandes projetos tiveram papel especialmente importante na expansão da IA. Ainda assim, o executivo acredita que o mercado não sofrerá consequências significativas com a saída do fundador da Nvidia. “Há tanta demanda, está tão claro que a IA é real, que as pessoas querem usá-la, e as receitas e a demanda estão crescendo tão fortemente que acredito que a indústria ficará bem”, afirmou. A avaliação contrasta com as preocupações de parte do mercado de tecnologia, que teme que a saída de Huang leve a Nvidia a rever os riscos financeiros assumidos para sustentar a expansão da infraestrutura de IA. Por enquanto, Altman prefere não opinar sobre o futuro do executivo na fabricante de chips. Sua avaliação é que, apesar da importância de Huang, o crescimento da IA não depende exclusivamente de sua permanência no comando da companhia. Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

sources.title: The open-source movement wants Jensen Huang back
sources.text: Supporters are signing a petition to reinstate Huang. But findings on Nvidia chips in China and a new Commerce rule are threatening open-source AI’s reputation and progress regardless. This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . On Friday, a petition to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia began circulating on social media, and by Monday it listed some notable signatories, including Elon Musk and several influential Nvidia researchers. But comb through the more than 115,000 names and you’ll notice a significant faction of Huang’s supporters—higher-ups from Hugging Face, a hub for sharing AI models, and venture capital firms Andreessen Horowitz and Sequoia Capital—come from a particular slice of the tech world. These names have a vested interest in the development of open-source AI, models that, unlike ChatGPT or Claude, can be downloaded and run independent of large tech companies. Supporters of such models say that concentrating AI in the hands of a few powerful companies will leave everyone else worse off (a concern that wouldn’t sound out of place among the AI industry's critics on the left, if so many open-source advocates weren’t also venture capitalists who stand to profit when startups can build on cheaper AI without paying Big Tech). Huang had become a sort of ringleader for those who defend open source to policymakers against concerns that such models come with no guardrails and cede AI leadership to China, where the most powerful and popular open-source models are created. They now want their most influential voice returned to his post. But it’s not just Huang’s extramarital affairs that threaten his (and Nvidia’s) credibility as an advocate for open-source AI. New research into China’s startups using Nvidia’s chips, and a new rule from the US Department of Commerce announced Monday, could deal a blow to both the movement’s reputation and its technical progress. On Thursday, the day Huang resigned, ex-OpenAI researcher Will DePue published findings online suggesting that China’s AI companies had far more access to Nvidia’s advanced Blackwell chips than previously estimated. China is banned from accessing Nvidia’s most cutting-edge chips to help protect America’s AI lead. It’s unclear how they would have gained access to the chips. DePue claims the results were verified by senior researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic, but an independent analysis has not confirmed the results. (DePue did not respond to a request for an interview. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.) The findings do not establish that Nvidia helped Chinese companies obtain the chips, and the broader problem of chip smuggling was already known to extend well beyond Nvidia’s control. But in suggesting that Nvidia may have profited from the rise of Chinese AI startups, whose models are increasingly being used by American companies instead of domestic alternatives, the findings do leave Huang in an awkward position. He has championed open-source AI as a way to strengthen American technological leadership. “Without open source, startups can’t thrive, university researchers can’t do research, you can’t teach AI, scientists can’t use AI,” he said last December during a talk about helping the US win the AI race against China. It also makes the idea of reinstating Huang even more of a long shot. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent even said last week that Nvidia should not consider someone from inside the company to replace him. The new findings lower Huang’s chances further. What happens next? Nvidia announced in September it would acquire Hugging Face for nearly $13 billion. Its support for open source also serves a straightforward financial interest: The more businesses that build their own models instead of forking over money to Anthropic and OpenAI, the more chips Nvidia can sell. But a new rule from the US Department of Commerce could mean the models popular on Hugging Face will soon stop getting smarter. The rule aims to prevent Chinese companies from training models on Nvidia chips that they can’t own directly, but that they can access remotely in data centers in countries like Malaysia—a workaround that has helped China’s open-source models get so good. The open-source world rallied around Huang because of his influence on policymakers. That was important, since the rise of China’s open-source models has splintered some in Trump’s orbit. If Huang is out, who is next? Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible. An exclusive interview with Nick Cammarata, the researcher whose 26,000-word viral blog post has AI safety folks celebrating. Breathless claims about AGI and new capabilities fall apart pretty quickly under scrutiny. With the rise of personal AI assistants, the internet isn't just for humans anymore. sources.name: CNBC Technology
sources.title: Nvidia board is not considering bringing Jensen Huang back as CEO, source tells CNBC
sources.text: Nvidia's board of directors is not considering bringing back Jensen Huang as CEO, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC. The board is focused on an investigation into Huang, and is not in discussions to bring him back, said the person, who spoke on condition of anonymity in order to discuss internal matters. Nvidia has hired law firm Wachtell Lipton to lead a probe into Huang's conduct and whether it compromised national security or company secrets. Last week, Huang resigned from Nvidia, the company he founded, after 33 years as CEO. The resignation came days after Huang admitted to an affair, and news stories alleged he had an affair with Alice Huang, who worked for a customer and is alleged to have contact with Chinese intelligence, as well as affairs with employees at Nvidia. Over the weekend, the Financial Times reported that Huang had discussed coming back with allies. Altimeter Capital's Brad Gerstner told CNBC on Monday that Huang had not discussed a comeback with him. A representative for Huang declined to comment on speculation on Sunday. Many in the tech world have called for Huang to return as Nvidia CEO. An online petition calling for his reinstatement has drawn 180,000 signatures as well as support from major figures including Elon Musk , Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney. President Donald Trump said on Monday that he is open to Jensen Huang returning as CEO of Nvidia. "It was not put at risk, and our country is now stronger than ever before," Trump told reporters when asked about U.S. national security concerns. On Friday, a representative for Nvidia's board said it was in the process of selecting a search firm for the Nvidia CEO role.

An online petition to bring Huang back as CEO has amassed more than 180,000 signatures , including from major figures like Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, and Replit CEO Amjad Masad. President Donald Trump said on Monday that it “certainly isn’t a bad idea” for Huang to return to Nvidia. A report from the Financial Times also suggests that Huang floated the idea of returning as CEO with some of his colleagues. Nvidia appointed its chief financial officer, Colette Kress, as interim CEO. The company has also hired Wachtell Lipton to investigate Huang’s conduct .

stories.title: Nvidia stock falls as investors price in fallout from Jensen Huang's resignation
stories.summary: Nvidia's stock continued to slide on Monday following the resignation of CEO Jensen Huang.

sources.name: CNBC Technology
sources.title: Nvidia stock falls as investors price in fallout from Jensen Huang's resignation
sources.text: Nvidia 's stock slid 4.12% Monday in the wake of CEO Jensen Huang 's resignation , leading a broader chipmaker selloff after the chip giant lost hundreds of billions in market cap last week. The continued decline since Huang's resignation brought Nvidia's stock to its lowest close since July 1, 2025. Huang resigned from Nvidia, the company's board announced on Thursday, after mounting scrutiny following reports that he had a relationship with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy. Huang told employees he had an affair in an email on Nov. 8. It was later reported that Huang had romantic relationships with two Nvidia employees. Nvidia did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on Friday. An online petition calling for Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO has drawn more than 170,000 signatures , as prominent tech executives, including Elon Musk , rallied behind him. A source familiar with the matter told CNBC, however, that Nvidia's board of directors is not considering bringing back Huang. Meanwhile, U.S. lawmakers are pushing to launch comprehensive investigations into the scandal. Huang cofounded Nvidia in 1993 and led the company through its meteoric rise to becoming the world's most valuable company, with its AI chips underpinning the technology's boom. Nvidia appointed longtime finance chief Colette Kress as interim CEO and said its board would consider both internal and external candidates in its search for a permanent successor. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday called for a "dramatic shakeup" at Nvidia, adding that the board should look outside the company for its next chief executive. He also suggested other Nvidia executives should face scrutiny over the chip giant's compliance with U.S. export controls. — CNBC's Caleigh Keating contributed to this report.

sources.name: Wired AI
sources.title: Nvidia Was Already in Trouble Before the Jensen Huang Mess
sources.text: Nvidia played a key role enabling the AI gold rush thanks in large part to its recently ousted CEO Jensen Huang . Huang was a master of foreseeing technological changes , investing in chips to train AI earlier than most. But just as he’s leaving , the company has a growing list of competitors with a range of new, advanced technology breathing down its neck. For Nvidia , where CFO Colette Kress has now taken the reins, the timing isn’t great. “Everything sold today was designed two to three years ago,” says the CEO of a large AI company, who spoke to WIRED on condition of anonymity to avoid hurting business relationships. Kress, or whoever replaces her permanently, will have to chart the course that the chip industry will take two years from now, the CEO says. Already, competitors have started to move in. Nvidia dominates the market for AI accelerators, capturing 80 percent of sales, according to Silicon Analysis. Longtime nemesis AMD is now making a concerted effort to build competitive AI chips. Its share of the market has crept up from just two percent in 2022 to between 7 and 10 percent in 2026. Big US cloud players—Google, Amazon, and Microsoft—are all developing more specialized chips to power the training and serving of AI models. Each has seen similar gains. These companies are designing their own silicon to reduce costs and to gain some independence from Nvidia. Several startups now offer more specialized chips that promise improvements over Nvidia’s core products. Cerebras, for instance, sells giant ones meant to power giant AI models. AMD recently bought Taalas, a company that burns models’ weights into silicon to make computations ultra efficient. Using these chips requires rewriting a lot of code, however, to make them work with cutting-edge AI models. Patrick Moorhead, chief analyst at MoorInStrat, a company that tracks the chip industry, says the rise of AI agents makes inference, or running models that have already been trained, more important. That’s an area where Nvidia has less of an edge compared to cloud hyperscalers and startups. Nvidia did, however, acquire a startup making specialized chips, called Groq, in December of 2025. And because of the rise in AI assistants and agents, there’s also growing demand for general purpose central processing units (CPUs), Moorhead said, an area where Nvidia barely competes. Nvidia still maintains a huge lead in AI thanks to Huang’s foresight. Huang cofounded the company in 1993 to design graphics chips for PCs. In the mid-2010s, he saw the promise of AI. He funded academic research on the topic, developed software to support AI engineering, and gave hardware to labs and startups. In 2022, ChatGPT took AI mainstream and sales of Nvidia chips skyrocketed. The company’s revenue went from $26.91 billion in January 2022 to $215.94 billion in January 2026. The challenges it faces may not be existential—but they do add up, especially on a global scale. While Nvidia’s fortunes have risen in the US, they have declined in the world’s other big market for AI: China. Washington is trying to restrict access to its most advanced chips, while Beijing is trying to develop its own chip industry. Nvidia is not allowed to sell its most powerful chips in China, but it can sell previous generations. Sales of these chips as well as non AI chips doubled over the past year, but China now accounts for only eight percent of the company’s overall revenue, compared with 20 percent in 2024, according to its fillings. It remains unclear how many chips exported to other countries may either end up in China or end up being used remotely by Chinese firms. Huawei, a Chinese tech giant targeted with US sanctions for several years, has developed new kinds of supercomputers that harness many more chips than usual to train and run AI models. Some Chinese AI companies, such as Z.ai, which makes one of the world’s best open source models, say they’ve trained their models entirely using Huawei’s chips. If Chinese open-weight models gain traction in other countries, it could create a market for Chinese chips elsewhere. Huang’s dealings with China played a major role in his downfall. He had a romantic relationship with Huang Le, also known as Alice Huang, a Chinese executive at a Singaporean company called Megaspeed who the US government suspects of being an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security. Megaspeed and its subsidiaries have reportedly imported between $4.6 and $7.5 billion Nvidia chips into southeast Asia. Reports suggest that the company may have provided access to the chips to Chinese AI firms. Babak Minovi, a senior analyst at the Eurasia Group, a consultancy that focuses on technology and geopolitics, says Huang was right to point out that cutting off access to China would empower domestic rivals. “Huang was taking a pragmatic line, and he knows competition,” he says. Even in markets that it dominates, Nvidia may turn out to be a victim of its own success. The AI models built using Nvidia’s chip are automating the very elements of coding, data analysis, and scientific research that help design chips. Most chip design firms use specialized AI models to arrange components on processors—something that traditionally required deep engineering expertise and experience. And both OpenAI and Anthropic have recently touted the ability of their newest models to design electronics from scratch. Moorhead says the shift towards AI chip design may not pose a huge threat to Nvidia because it’s riding the same wave. “They have access to AI too,” he notes. But Moorhead says the way AI models can now quickly rewrite code to run on different hardware may prove a problem. For years, Nvidia has attracted developers by providing software that makes it easy to write programs and build models for its silicon. stories.title: How we make Together AI easy for coding agents to use
stories.summary: We built agent evals to test how effective coding agents are at using Together AI. Small fixes to our docs, skills, and API errors lifted task completion rate from 75% to 97%.

sources.name: Together AI
sources.title: How we make Together AI easy for coding agents to use
sources.text: Earlier this year, we started seeing more and more devs using coding agents to build with Together AI. It’s not hard to see why: It might take days or even weeks for a developer to wire up an app for production inference by hand, especially if they’re new to the platform. But for an agent using our SDK and CLI, it only takes a few minutes—at least in theory. In practice, we had no idea whether the agents pointed at our platform were able to work with Together efficiently, or if they were hitting obstacles, going down rabbit holes or failing outright, and wasting tokens in the process. As devs delegate more of their work to agents, developer experience (DX) is increasingly becoming synonymous with agent experience (AX). The easier your software is for agents to use, the easier it is for devs to build it into their own products and workflows. GitHub is a textbook example of great AX: activity on the platform has tripled in the past year, with agents opening about 40% of all PRs in 2026 (and, we’re willing to bet, writing a lot more than 40% of the lines of code across all commits). This is thanks to GitHub’s phenomenal API, CLI, and docs, all of which make it exceptionally easy for agents to use. (This writer was not even aware GitHub had a CLI until agents started using it for him, and now he probably uses it 1000+ times a day). To improve our AX at Together AI, we needed a way to measure how agent-ready our platform actually was. In this post, we’ll walk through how we run agent evals, two problems they uncovered and how we fixed them, and what we’ve learned. Before we could start evaluating, we needed to know what agents were actually being asked to do … so we could, y’know, figure out if they could do those things. We started building a list of common tasks that developers tackle on Together, like running a batch inference job, building a voice agent, or managing autoscaling for an inference endpoint. By task, we really just mean a prompt, something you’d tell an agent to do—for example: The prompt asks for both availability and pricing, without mentioning that these details live in two different places. This is realistic, as the average user probably doesn’t know up front where each piece of information lives, which could easily trip up both humans and agents. After building our list of tasks, we run each one of them three ways: Each full evaluation runs every task against each agent configuration using three models, with two attempts at each task—so six attempts per task for each config, as shown here for our run on September 30th: When we started building our evals, we ran everything by hand: open a new terminal, paste a prompt into Claude Code, let the agent do its thing (or fail to do its thing), and repeat for each configuration. It was manual and tedious, so once we figured out the shape of the system we wanted, we started automating it. Now we run each agent in a Together sandbox so they don’t interfere with our local environment or each other. GitHub Actions handles setup, starts the agent, cleans up afterward, and saves the results, while a proxy handles the agent's requests to the Together API and records the activity, so we can see which endpoints the agent calls and what comes back. After a run finishes, an LLM judge reviews the task prompt and the recorded session, then assigns one of three verdicts: Failed and incomplete verdicts don’t necessarily tell us whether the problem was with the agent, the API, or missing evidence. They just tell us where to start looking. We investigate passing runs too. An agent can often work around confusing responses and still finish, and those recoveries show us what to fix to improve token efficiency. To make that review practical, we built a results viewer that compares how different models and configs performed. For each run, it shows the prompt, the tools the agent used, the responses it got back, and any API activity: Remember the GPU cluster task from earlier? Seems pretty simple, but when we ran our evals early last summer, Sonnet 4.6 passed only 4 of 15 attempts at this task, even with skills enabled. Our post-mortem revealed the same pattern in the failed runs: Sonnet treated the sample output in our CLI reference, which listed a single region and two GPU types, as if it were the live inventory. It also skipped the regions lookup and named what it thought was the cheapest option without ever checking the pricing page. The problems were on our end. First, the sample output wasn’t properly labeled, so nothing told the agent to run the command to retrieve the relevant data. Second, our skill file linked to the GPU clusters marketing page rather than the pricing table, so Sonnet opened the marketing page, didn’t see any real prices, and just made a best-effort guess at the cheapest GPU available. More capable models were able to work around the issue. In that same period, Opus 4.8 passed 13 of 14 attempts using the same config. According to the transcript, it noticed that the list_regions response didn't include prices, so it kept searching until it found them in our docs. This is why it’s crucial to test your product with less capable models; if we had only tested with Opus, it would have taken us much longer to find the gap. To fix it, we isolated the failure by pulling the GPU clusters skill out of the full skill package, and wrote a narrower prompt that reproduced only this issue. It failed every time when tested against the old skill file, so we had reliable repro steps (use the old skill), and an easy way to test each new version (update the skill). We went through several iterations until we landed on a small change: two new sentences in the skill that point the agent to the pricing table, and explain how to use it with the live regions API: After this change, the task passed 100% of the time for all models we tested using the skill-enabled config. The same GPU task also turned up a problem in our API. In a recent baseline run,

sources.title: TokenEconomizer: Learning from Experience to Make AI Coding Agents More Efficient
sources.text: By Aaron J. Li , Research Intern Weijia Xu , Senior Researcher Chandan Singh , Staff Research Scientist Zixiao Chen Jeevana Priya Inala , Senior Researcher Bin Yu , Professor Ion Stoica , Professor Michel Galley , Senior Principal Research Manager Jianfeng Gao , Technical Fellow & Corporate Vice President AI coding agents are increasingly helping developers fix bugs and build features largely on their own, but every interaction with their models consumes tokens. In each session , an agent sends instructions, tool descriptions, and session history to its model. Most efforts to reduce this cost focus on individual tasks. Yet developers return to the same repositories, giving agents an opportunity to learn from previous work. Without that learning, an agent may repeatedly rediscover how to run tests, load tools it never uses, or spend dozens of turns revisiting the same error. In our paper, TokenEconomizer: Experience-Driven Black-Box Cost Control for Coding Agents , we ask a simple question: can experience in a repository help an agent solve future tasks more efficiently? TokenEconomizer, an open-source plugin from UC Berkeley, Microsoft Research, and Microsoft Security, turns completed sessions into guidance for subsequent ones. It reduces waste without changing the agent or its underlying model, so developers can use it alongside the coding agents they already rely on. We first profiled Claude Code on 60 tasks from SWE-Bench, a benchmark of real bug fixes in open-source Python projects, running each repository’s tasks in sequence. Three kinds of waste recurred: We also tested three popular open-source plugins, each built around a fixed cost-saving strategy. Each lowered costs in some repositories but not others. Together, these findings suggest that effective cost control must adapt to the repository, rather than apply the same strategy everywhere. Join Microsoft’s Peter Lee on a journey to discover how AI is impacting healthcare and what it means for the future of medicine. After each session, TokenEconomizer reads the session’s log and updates what it knows about the repository. It then acts through three mechanisms, using only interfaces the agent already provides, as illustrated in Figure 2. Micro-skills capture repository-specific knowledge in one-line notes. TokenEconomizer identifies recurring patterns across sessions and proposes corresponding notes. They are added to the agent’s starting context only after several sessions have confirmed the pattern, and retires the note if later evidence contradicts it. Tool pruning removes tools that repository history suggests the agent is unlikely to use , while always retaining core tools for running commands and editing files. Removed tools can be restored if needed. Failure-loop intervention watches for an agent that keeps hitting the same failure. A judge model decides whether the agent is truly stuck or still making progress. If it is stuck, the agent gets a short note suggesting a different approach. In the open-source plugin, if the agent is still stuck after the note, TokenEconomizer alerts the developer rather than stopping the work itself. The controller is designed to revise its decisions as new evidence arrives. Reported savings also account for the cost of TokenEconomizer’s own model calls. We evaluated TokenEconomizer on 277 SWE-Bench tasks from six repositories, using five different AI coding agent and model combinations. For each repository, TokenEconomizer started with no prior session history. TokenEconomizer lowered the average cost by 18.4–30.9%, as shown in Figure 3, and saved the most in all 30 repository-combination pairs without performance loss. By contrast, lowering the model’s reasoning effort saved similar or larger amounts but led to substantial performance degradation. Savings grow as experience accumulates. Early tasks can cost more while TokenEconomizer learns, but cumulative costs fell below the default in every repository by the sixth task, shown inFigure 4. Each mechanism contributes savings on its own, and combining all three delivers the largest reduction. The savings also carried over to sequential web development, with costs 16.0–21.2% lower on Web-Bench. On security auditing, where every task is in a new repository, costs were 6.4–19.6% lower. TokenEconomizer opens a path toward coding agents that learn not only how to solve tasks, but also how to spend computation more effectively. Its lightweight controller shows how experience can improve efficiency without changing the underlying agent or model. The open-source plugin makes these directions accessible to developers and researchers. It is designed to run alongside existing AI coding agents without modifying their underlying models, requires no API key of its own, and keeps what it learns on the developer’s machine. We invite the community to use it as a starting point for exploring agents that become more resourceful with experience, adapting how they work, as well as what they know. Technical Fellow & Corporate Vice President

sources.title: Jensen Huang discute un posible retorno a la dirección de Nvidia, según 'FT'
sources.text: Jensen Huang , cofundador de Nvidia , estaría discutiendo con posibles aliados un potencial regreso a la dirección de la compañía que ayudó a crear en 1993 y de la que era consejero delegado hasta su renuncia el pasado jueves tras salir a la luz varias infidelidades , incluida una relación con una presunta espía china, además de con una subordinada. Según informa Financial Times , que cita fuentes conocedoras, el carismático líder tecnológico estaría considerando la posibilidad de regresar como CEO de Nvidia , mientras aliados en Silicon Valley presionan a la junta directiva de la compañía, que está realizando una investigación interna sobre la conducta del ejecutivo, para que lo reincorpore días después de que se viera forzado a renunciar al cargo. En este sentido, un aliado de Huang declaró al periódico que estaban organizando un grupo de trabajo con ejecutivos de Silicon Valley para presionar de cara al regreso del exconsejero delegado de Nvidia para lo que intentarían obtener el apoyo de la Casa Blanca . "Todos los que importan en el sector tecnológico fuera de los laboratorios de vanguardia admiran a Jensen ", afirmó, añadiendo que el propio Huang apoyaba estos esfuerzos. Una campaña pública para restituir al CEO de Nvidia ha cobrado fuerza durante el fin de semana al sumar a personalidades como Elon Musk , CEO de Tesla y SpaceX, y Tim Sweeney , consejero delegado de Epic Games , a los ejecutivos que respaldaron una carta pública reclamando que la junta directiva "Traiga de vuelta a Jensen". Brad Gerstner , fundador de Altimeter Capital , y Gavin Baker , director de Atreides Management , ambos accionistas de Nvidia, publicaron el viernes una carta abierta en la que pedían al consejo de administración de la compañía considerar "todas las opciones, incluido el posible regreso de Jensen Huang". Asimismo, el diario destaca que Huang sigue gozando de una lealtad inquebrantable entre algunos empleados , varios de los cuales han manifestado públicamente su petición de regreso tras su renuncia. No obstante, advierte que cualquier intento de restituirle al frente de Nvidia probablemente se enfrente a la oposición de importantes legisladores en Washington , mientras que el secretario del Tesoro de EEUU , Scott Bessent, pidió este domingo una " reorganización drástica " en el liderazgo de la empresa tras la salida de Huang. A este respecto, el periódico apunta que, incluso los aliados de Huang dudaban sobre cómo rehabilitar la reputación del ex CEO de la empresa, ya que "tener una relación extramatrimonial con una subordinada es motivo de despido ", según reconoció una persona involucrada en los esfuerzos por la readmisión de Huang. El pasado jueves, junto con la renuncia de Jensen Huang como consejero delegado, Nvidia anunció la designación como máxima ejecutiva interina de Colette Kress , actual vicepresidenta ejecutiva y directora financiera de la empresa, hasta que se complete el proceso de sucesión , para lo que el consejo de administración comenzó la búsqueda de un sustituto, teniendo en cuenta candidatos tanto internos como externos. A este respecto, Financial Times informó de que la junta de Nvidia se ha puesto en contacto con René Haas , consejero delegado de Arm , como posible sucesor de Huang. sources.title: Jensen Huang discute retorno como CEO da Nvidia e líderes tech lançam abaixo-assinado
sources.text: A divisão gamer da Nvidia pode acabar? Saiba o futuro da linha GeForce após saída de Jensen Huang A renúncia de Jensen Huang ao cargo de CEO da Nvidia, oficializada na última quinta-feira (12) , está longe de virar um assunto encerrado na indústria. Até mesmo o próprio executivo, segundo o Financial Times , agora está reconsiderando tentar voltar ao cargo. De acordo com a reportagem, Huang teria discutido com pessoas próximas a possibilidade de retornar à cadeira de gerente executivo. Uma das fontes citou até a montagem de uma “sala de guerra” formada por executivos do Vale do Silício para iniciar um lobby a favor da restituição. Um dos objetivos do grupo é conseguir o apoio da Casa Branca , que é uma peça bastante interessada no futuro da Nvidia. Por ser um dos pilares do setor de inteligência artificial (IA) e uma das empresa mais valiosas do mundo, ela tem papel relevante em negociações com marcas locais e estrangeiras. “Todo mundo que importa no mundo da tecnologia fora dos laboratórios de modelos de fronteira ama o Jensen”, teria dito uma pessoa próxima ao assunto. Até o momento, tanto a Nvidia quanto o próprio Huang não se manifestaram sobre a reportagem. Huang renunciou na última semana após a revelação de que ele manteve dois casos extraconjugais: um relacionamento com uma executiva que pode ser uma espiã chinesa , uma diretora de divisão da Nvidia e possivelmente outra funcionária ainda identificada também da empresa de chips. Funcionários da companhia estão se manifestando em chats internos pedindo uma possível volta do executivo ao cargo para o conselho de diretores da marca, que ainda está investigando o caso. Além disso, um abaixo-assinado que pede ao conselho o retorno de Huang ao menos enquanto o relatório não for divulgado já tem mais de 175 mil assinaturas. Além de fãs e funcionários, ela tem apoio inclusive de figuras como Elon Musk , Tim Sweeney (CEO da Epic Games) e Garry Tan, CEO da incubadora de startups Y Combinator. Quem exatamente é Dario Amodei, CEO da Anthropic e prestes a realizar o maior IPO da história? Entenda nesta matéria ! /Com informações de Financial Times. stories.summary: CEO ousted after affair with suspected Chinese spy reportedly plans comeback, but US treasury secretary urges ‘dramatic shake-up’ Megaspeed says it’s a ‘legitimate and lawful business’ Business live – latest updates Elon Musk and a host of other tech bosses have called for Jensen Huang’s reinstatement at Nvidia, amid reports the former chief executive is already plotting a return to the chip...

sources.name: The Guardian Technology
sources.title: Elon Musk joins 165,000 others calling for Nvidia to bring back Jensen Huang in open letter
sources.text: CEO ousted after affair with suspected Chinese spy reportedly plans comeback, but US treasury secretary urges ‘dramatic shake-up’ Megaspeed says it’s a ‘legitimate and lawful business’ Elon Musk and a host of other tech bosses have called for Jensen Huang’s reinstatement at Nvidia, amid reports the former chief executive is already plotting a return to the chip company just four days after his resignation. An open letter that has more than 165,000 signatories demands that the company’s board members “bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts”. Huang’s resignation on Thursday ended a 33-year run at the helm of the AI company he co-founded, after reports he had at least two extramarital affairs, one with a woman accused of spying for China and another with a subordinate. According to the Financial Times , Huang has discussed a possible return to the company with people close to him. One Huang ally told the paper they were putting together ⁠a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby ​for the former Nvidia ‌CEO’s return ‌and would try to garner support from ‌the White House. “Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen,” the person said, adding that the efforts had Huang’s support. On Friday, two big shareholders, the investors Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker, urged the board to keep “all options” open. In Washington, however, the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, argued on Sunday that Nvidia should look outside the company for its next CEO. “They need a dramatic shake-up,” Bessent said on Fox News. Bessent also called on Nvidia to explain whether it had knowingly allowed its most advanced AI chips to reach China, saying this was more important than Huang’s affair with the alleged spy for Beijing, Alice Huang. The US forbids sales to China of the most cutting-edge AI chips as parts of its strategy to stay ahead of Beijing in the race to dominate artificial intelligence. In late 2025, Trump authorised sales of Nvidia chips called H200s to China, but not the most advanced chips used to run AI models reshaping modern society. “Nothing above the H200s can be sold to the Chinese,” Bessent said, adding that it was important to examine “whether Nvidia had a culture of compliance around the US export restrictions”. Bessent said he wanted answers from Nvidia and its internal investigation of Jensen Huang’s behaviour within the next 10 days. One analyst downplayed the prospect of a Huang return, describing the notion of the ex-CEO’s reinstatement as “ridiculous”. Dan Ives, an analyst at Yorkville Ives, said the range of issues facing Huang and Nvidia, from personal conduct to questions over China, made an external candidate or the permanent appointment of the interim CEO – Nvidia’s chief financial officer, Colette Kress – the best option. “We see no chance Jensen comes back to Nvidia as CEO and for the company the best path forward is with a new external CEO or Colette,” he said, describing the petition as “noise and distraction”. US lawmakers have said Donald Trump’s administration must answer questions on what it knew about Huang’s relationship with the suspected Chinese spy. Jensen Huang has agreed to appear before the House select committee on China, as well as the foreign affairs and the intelligence committees. The dates of the appearances, likely to be behind closed doors, have not been confirmed. On Sunday, Megaspeed, the Singapore-based company where Alice Haung was an executive until she left in 2025, said it was a “ legitimate and lawful business ”. In the past three years, the company was one of Nvidia’s biggest foreign customers, buying nearly $5bn (£3.8bn) in AI chips and advanced hardware. Alongside Musk, the tech heavyweight signatories on the letter calling for Jensen Huang’s return include Tim Sweeney, the founder and CEO of the video game publisher Epic Games, and Garry Tan, the president of Y Combinator, San Francisco’s most renowned business incubator. Another signatory, the Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, wrote that Huang had “erred, yes – to err is to be human – but I do not believe anything he has done rises to the bar of separating him from his company”. More than 7,500 signatories identified themselves as Nvidia employees, equivalent to 18% of the company’s workforce. The support illustrates the unique standing of Huang, who is seen within the industry as a godfather of AI . Under his leadership, Nvidia became a pivotal Silicon Valley investor, financing datacentres and startups, earning it the nickname “the central bank of AI”. But the company – which will report on its quarterly earnings on Tuesday – has also faced criticism that it has fuelled a speculative investment bubble. Huang fought any constraints on the AI race, clashing on these issues with the Claude creator, Anthropic, and its chief executive, Dario Amodei. Agence France-Presse and Reuters contributed to this report

sources.title: Reviravolta: Jensen Huang articula retorno à NVIDIA com apoio de Elon Musk e Tim Sweeney
sources.text: Por André Lourenti Magalhães • Editado por Jones Oliveira | 16/11/2026 às 14:02 Jensen Huang renunciou ao cargo de CEO da NVIDIA na última semana, mas não descarta voltar ao comando da empresa. De acordo com o site Financial Times, Huang conta com aliados no Vale do Silício para pressionar o conselho da Big Tech sobre um possível retorno . Uma das fontes ouvidas pela reportagem original afirma que há uma “sala de guerra” montada por parceiros e lobistas para trazê-lo de volta ao cargo. Há até a possibilidade de buscar apoio na Casa Branca, ainda que o caminho seja improvável — o Secretário do Tesouro dos EUA, Scott Bessent, já defendeu publicamente uma reestruturação na empresa de chips. Um dos argumentos dos aliados é de que Jensen Huang é uma pessoa querida no mercado de tecnologia. Outras fontes afirmam que o ex-CEO era o responsável por conduzir negociações importantes no mercado de IA. Um eventual retorno é apoiado até por funcionários da própria NVIDIA : comentários em caixa de sugestões internas da companhia defendem a volta do executivo. Por enquanto, a companhia é liderada de forma interina por Colette Kress, que atuava como vice-presidente executiva e diretora financeira antes da mudança. Jensen Huang também é defendido por nomes importantes do mercado, como Elon Musk e o CEO da Epic Games, Tim Sweeney . Ambos assinaram uma carta aberta pedindo para o conselho “trazer Jensen de volta” . A NVIDIA ainda não tem novas atualizações sobre o comando da empresa, mas rumores apontam que o CEO da Arm, Rene Haas, seria um dos favoritos a assumir a cadeira deixada por Huang. Jensen Huang renunciou ao cargo após confirmar um caso extraconjugal com a ex-diretora da Megaspeed International e empresária Alice Huang, acusada de espionagem a favor da China.
